questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presented with 2 days of bloody diarrhea. She worked as a school teacher and had led a school trip to a farm 4 days before her symptoms began. She had a history of mild asthma and used occasional salbutamol inhalers as needed. She had no known allergies. She had not received any recent steroids or antibiotics. On admission she was dehydrated. Her temperature was 36.8°C, and she was diffusely tender on abdominal examination. She had a seizure shortly after admission and developed some motor weakness. Investigations: Creatinine clearance 42 mL/min Peripheral white cell count 14.0 ×109/L Hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL Platelet count 90,000/μL CT scan abdomen findings consistent with pseudomembranous colitis Supportive management with IV fluids was commenced
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?
questions.explanation: Send stool for enteric pathogens (culture/NAAT) This patient has enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC, also called Shiga toxin-producing E. coli or STEC) causing bloody diarrhea following contact with a petting farm. This has caused hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) with renal failure, thrombocytopenia, and microangiopathic anemia. HUS can occur in 6%–9% of EHEC infections, and this patient also has neurologic symptoms. EHEC is also a rare cause of pseudomembranous colitis when culture-negative for Clostridioides difficile. Antibiotic treatment is contraindicated pending stool culture results and may make symptoms worse. Hence supportive treatment is advised. There are also likely to be other patients on the excursion who may be affected, and this should be further investigated as part of a possible outbreak.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q15

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presented with 3 days of diarrhea and severe abdominal pain. She was living in Texas but had traveled to Mexico to visit family 2 weeks prior to presentation. The patient reported drinking raw milk routinely and had a 3-year-old daughter in daycare. Investigations: Multiplex gastrointestinal panel PCR: positive for Shiga toxin 2
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Monitor for development of HUS Although E. coli O157 is the serotype most commonly associated with HUS, any serotype can cause HUS. There is no reason to rule out O157 since the patient should be monitored for HUS regardless of serotype. The presence of Shiga toxin 1 or Shiga toxin 2 is indicative of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC), not Shigella. If Shigella was present, it would have been detected as Shigella. A Shigella-specific target is part of all currently available GI panels. Antimicrobial treatment of STEC has historically been associated with worse outcomes. There are some newer data that refute this dogma, but the standard practice is still to avoid antimicrobials for STEC.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q1

questions.question: 19. A patient presents with abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Diagnosed with E. coli O157.

parts.text: What is the pathogenesis of this infection (1.5)
What are three clinical or laboratory features of this infection? (1.5)
What are three risk factors for development of HUS? (1.5)
Explain how antibiotics can cause HUS (0.5)

cohort_answer.text: Pathogenesis: Shiga toxin production; STEC with Shiga toxin 2 and variants more virulent than Shiga toxin 1 alone. Clinical/lab features: incubation 1-10 days; initially nonbloody diarrhea becomes bloody 1-3 days after onset, often without persistent fever, usually abdo pain, typically resolves in 7 days; often elevated leuks and thrombocytosis. HUS risk factors: age (elderly >75 and younger than 10, also cited <5yrs/>65yrs), immunosuppression, use of antimotility agents in last 2 weeks, initial WBC >13, antibiotic use (highest if within first 3 days of illness). Antibiotics and HUS: in vitro, antibiotics cause E. coli to release Shiga toxin from injured bacteria in the intestine, making toxin more available for absorption

questions.question: Ecoli 0157H7 outbreak in nursing home. 35 people affected.

parts.text: Name 2 patient centered interventions, 2 staff interventions 1 environmental intervention.
Given outbreak curve. What is the outbreak curve?
What is the incubation period based on the outbreak curve.

questions.model_answer: a) Two patient-centered interventions: (1) Contact precautions/cohorting of symptomatic residents. (2) Enhanced hand hygiene assistance for residents (many unable to independently perform hand hygiene) and exclusion from communal dining/activities while symptomatic. Two staff interventions: (1) Reinforced hand hygiene and use of gloves/gowns for contact precautions when caring for affected residents. (2) Exclusion of symptomatic staff from work until cleared (per public health/local policy, e.g. 48 hours symptom-free and/or negative stool clearance). One environmental intervention: enhanced cleaning/disinfection of high-touch surfaces and shared equipment/bathrooms with an appropriate disinfectant. b) Outbreak curve: propagated (person-to-person) epidemic curve - shows a series of progressively larger waves/peaks spaced roughly one incubation period apart, reflecting ongoing secondary transmission (consistent with spread from 4 initial cases to 35, characteristic of person-to-person/fecal-oral transmission in an institutional setting). c) Incubation period based on the outbreak curve: approximately 3-4 days (consistent with the interval between successive case clusters/peaks).

questions.question: E coli O157:H7 outbreak in a nursing home spreads from 4 patients initially to involve 35 patients.

parts.text: Give 2 resident-associated IPC measures
2 staff associated IPC measures
1 environment related IPC measure
Given an epi curve and asked to give the pattern (propagated); give a host and pathogen factor leading to this epi curve pattern; what is the incubation period based on the epi curve?

questions.model_answer: a) Two resident-associated IPC measures: (1) Contact precautions and cohorting/isolation of symptomatic residents. (2) Assistance with and reinforcement of hand hygiene for residents, with exclusion from communal areas/dining while symptomatic. b) Two staff-associated IPC measures: (1) Strict hand hygiene and use of gloves/gown (contact precautions) when providing care. (2) Exclusion of ill staff from work (furlough) until cleared per public health guidance. c) One environmental IPC measure: enhanced terminal cleaning and disinfection of shared surfaces, bathrooms, and equipment. d) Epi curve pattern: propagated (multiple successive peaks each roughly one incubation period apart), reflecting ongoing person-to-person/fecal-oral transmission rather than a single common-source exposure. Host factor: close congregate living with shared caregivers/bathrooms and residents often incontinent/dependent on staff for hygiene, facilitating secondary transmission. Pathogen factor: very low infectious dose of E. coli O157:H7 (as few as 10-100 organisms) allows efficient person-to-person spread. Incubation period from the epi curve: approximately 3-4 days.

questions.question: E. coli O157 outbreak.

parts.text: What are 2 resident, 2 staff, and 1 site specific intervention?
[image-based question: outbreak epidemic curve graph] What type of outbreak is evidenced in this image?
[image-based question: outbreak epidemic curve graph] What is the incubation period based on the graph?
What is a pathogen and a host criteria necessary for this outbreak?

questions.model_answer: a) Interventions: Resident (2) - cohort/isolate symptomatic residents with contact precautions, exclude symptomatic residents from communal dining/activities. Staff (2) - exclude ill staff from work until cleared, reinforce hand hygiene (soap and water, not just alcohol gel, for enteric pathogens). Site (1) - enhanced environmental cleaning/disinfection of shared surfaces and bathrooms. b) Outbreak curve type: point-source (common-source) outbreak - a single sharp peak. c) Incubation period: estimated from the interval between the presumed exposure and the peak/median onset of cases on the curve (typically 3-4 days for E. coli O157). d) Host factor: susceptible/immunocompromised or extremes-of-age host (e.g., elderly residents). Pathogen factor: low infectious dose of E. coli O157:H7 allowing person-to-person/fecal-oral spread.

questions.question: Outbreak! Of E.coli. A curve is shown. The peaks are q4d.

parts.text: What interventions? (2 for residents, 2 for staff, 1 for environment)
List 4 of the steps in an outbreak investigation
What are 1 host and 1 pathogen factor that explain the above curve.

questions.model_answer: a) Interventions - Residents (2): contact precautions/cohorting of ill residents, exclusion from communal activities/dining. Staff (2): exclusion of ill staff from work, reinforced hand hygiene with soap and water. Environment (1): enhanced terminal cleaning/disinfection of high-touch surfaces. b) Steps in outbreak investigation (4): (1) confirm the outbreak/diagnosis (2) define a case and identify cases (line listing) (3) describe the outbreak by person/place/time (epidemic curve) (4) implement control measures and evaluate their effectiveness. c) Host factor for q4d peaks: ongoing susceptible population (new residents/staff becoming exposed each cycle). Pathogen factor: incubation period of E. coli O157 (~3-4 days) matching the recurring peaks, consistent with continued person-to-person transmission.

Three clinical or laboratory features.
Three risk factors for HUS
Why does antibiotic treatment potentially worsen/cause HUS?

cohort_answer.text:
E coli releases shiga toxin into bloodstream; Toxins causes endothelial damage especially in renal cells; Endothelial damage causes pro-coagulant and inflammatory cascade; Platelet form microthrombus at sites of damage thus blocking vessels; RBCs are destroyed when they flow through areas with mircothrombus, leading to haemolytic anaemia, schistocytes and renal damage
Thrombocytopenia; Elevated urea; Haemolytic anaemia; Bloody diarrhea
Age <5yo; Receiving abx; High WBC at presentation

cohort_answer.text:
EHEC produces STX1 or STX2 toxins which bind GB3 receptors in endothelial cells, highly concentrated in renal tissue. These recruit leukocytes, can prompt apoptosis, elicit formation of microthrombi and impaired fibrinolysis; may also have secondary activation of complement
Antibiotic use (specifically fluoroquinolones) - due to increased release/production of toxin during diarrheal phase; High leukocyte count >13; <5 years old; Female; Vomiting; fever
